title: Francis Bacon and the Birth of the Modern Scientific Method (1620)
explainer: In 1620, the English philosopher and statesman Francis Bacon published the Novum Organum, arguing that reliable knowledge comes from systematically collecting observations and reasoning upward from them (induction), rather than reasoning downward from accepted first principles the way Aristotle's logic had taught for centuries. Bacon's insistence on deliberately gathering evidence before forming a theory is an early ancestor of the hypothesis-and-experiment discipline that research methodology still runs on, even though his own fact-cataloguing method was later superseded.

title: Karl Popper and Falsifiability
explainer: Writing in the mid-20th century, the philosopher Karl Popper argued that what makes a claim scientific is not that evidence can confirm it, but that it could in principle be shown false by some observation — a standard now called falsifiability. For anyone doing original research, Popper's point reframes good methodology as actively designing tests that could prove your own hypothesis wrong, rather than only collecting examples that support it.
